paragraphs: […] What was said in the Torah of Moses — which is this very Torah, no other — and what contradicts their [Rabbanite] position on the Sabbath, by way of stringency and license, and likewise in matters of food and rulings and so on.

We return to the systematic exposition of our position: God addressed His servants in the language their intellects could grasp — within their natural capacity and constitution. When God (mighty and exalted) wished to inform His servants that visible things are not concealed from Him, He spoke — within the framework of human convention, in which everything visible is perceived by the sense of sight — in terms of the eye; not that there is an organ that is an eye. Likewise, when He wished to inform them that audible things are not concealed from Him, He described Himself with reference to the ear, the sense-organ of hearing. He described Himself with mouth and lips, since in human discourse this is how speech is carried out — and God speaks to some of His creatures. He described Himself with heart, since He is wise — and in the observable, the seat of wisdom is the heart.

Scripture's idiom (Isa 38:17): "behind His back" — this is a figurative locution, parallel to a person saying "throw this matter behind your back," meaning: pay it no attention, do not bother with it; as also (Ezek 23:35), "and thou hast cast me behind thy back," meaning: you rejected Me through your disobedience and paid no attention to My word. As to hand and arm: these refer to power, as is clear from many passages — Exod 14:31, "and Israel saw the great power that the Lord wrought upon Egypt";[{2}] and many more, beyond enumeration. As to finger: cf. Exod 8:15, when Pharaoh's magicians said, "this is the finger of God" — meaning the power of God. As to right hand: it indicates might, strength, dominion. As to leg / foot: it means He prevails, all things are beneath Him; since every conquered thing is referred to as being under the foot — as Solomon said of his father David (1 Kgs 5:17): "until the Lord put them under the soles of his feet," meaning not that they were trampled, but that the Lord made David prevail over them so that they were like a thing trodden under foot.

As to the inwards/bowels of God: he means He is gentle and merciful; standing = not negligent, supportive; sitting = steadfast, abiding; anger = He punishes and avenges; jealousy/vengeance = He will eventually exact retribution, even if delayed; satisfaction = He rewards obedience; joy = the one who has earned the desired action has reached the most exalted place; for whoever rejoices in something has attained desire and contentment. The word yiśmaḥ (will rejoice) is also used in another sense — will appear / be manifest: cf. Prov 13:9, "the light of the righteous rejoices" (i.e., appears, shines); and similarly Ps 104:31, "the Lord shall rejoice in His works" — to be read: the Lord shall appear by His works, meaning that His works indicate Him. His creating-handiwork manifests Him to creation.

All the language about God's regret (nidamānu in some prophetic texts) means that the outcome about which the regret is said has reached the limit of repugnance, reached the extreme of evil — such that regret was due upon its occurrence. The Creator (exalted) does not properly regret; for regret arises in one who is ignorant of the consequences of his actions; when he does something whose unintended result he dislikes, he regrets his action. But God is not ignorant of consequences — He knows all that will ever be — and therefore cannot truly regret. As Scripture itself says (1 Sam 15:29): "and also the Glory of Israel will not lie nor repent"; also: "for He is not a man, that He should repent"; and Balaam's statement (Num 23:19): "God is not man, that He should lie, nor son of man, that He should repent." Parallel to what we said about joy = the Lord shall manifest by His works (Ps 104:31).

Isa 5:2: "He hoped that it would yield grapes; but it yielded wild grapes" — meaning that they were in such a state that good could have been expected of them, on the basis of which reward and kindness would have come to them; instead, their bad action reversed the expected outcome. Ps 132:14 ("it is My desired-resting-place") — which suggests desire — refers to His will; love is of the genus of acceptance-of-the-act. Mal 3:4 ("pleasing unto the Lord") — which suggests enjoyment and delight — refers to acceptance and reception; the act has become in the state of acceptance analogous to what is enjoyed. Gen 8:21 ("and the Lord smelt the sweet savor") — refers also to acceptance; cf. the negative parallel Lev 26:31, "I will not accept nor smell your offerings," and Ezek 20:41, "by the savor of your delight will I accept you." As to Deut 32:27 ("were it not that I feared the wrath of the enemy") — fear in the language can refer to avoidance and abstention from a possible thing. We say "so-and-so is always fearful" meaning alert, not negligent, will not be caught in something he dislikes.

Ps 44:24 ("Awake! why dost thou sleep, O Lord") — means: rouse Yourself in our cause and end it by giving us release, rescuing us from what we are in; cf. Ps 35:23, "stir up Thyself and awake to my judgment, O my God." A person may say to his friend, who is not asleep: "pay attention to your matter," meaning look into what you are in and take care of it. Scripture itself negates sleep and slumber of God (Ps 121:4): "Behold, He that keepeth Israel shall neither slumber nor sleep."

All of God's "coming and going, walking, riding, passing" refers to power and sakīna (the divine indwelling presence) and the lights and angelic processions of the heavenly hosts — which are the armies of the angels. For if it were a literal going-out, stepping, passing, dwelling — then His essence would be located in one place and not another. But Scripture itself tells us that He fills every place (Jer 23:24): "Do I not fill the heavens and the earth?" And David (Ps 139:8): "If I ascend up into heaven, Thou art there." Both passages indicate He fills heaven and earth in every place by [the] guidance and the indwelling of [His] power, not by the indwelling of His essence. For indwelling of essence is impossible — were it so, every place would cut through the divine essence; the celestial sphere would separate between what is above it and what is below it; the earth would similarly divide the essence into parts. This is the height of corruption and falsehood.

Idioms like (Exod 24:10), "they saw the God of Israel" — the term "seeing" applies in language to knowing, as Gen 42:1, "and Jacob saw that there was sufficient food in Egypt" — i.e., he came to know. Scripture's reports of this kind mean that the one about whom this is said experienced, at that time, some demonstration or sign of divine action — manifestation of power, miracle — from which something at the time, or to come, was inferred. Each instance is to be explained in its proper place. Some have also interpreted seeing in another sense, parallel to a person saying "I have seen God say in His book such-and-such," meaning I understand, from His book; or "so-and-so will you give your view on such-and-such?" meaning what is your considered judgment?

Isa 6:1: "I saw the Lord sitting on a throne" suggests place. The intent is to describe the greatness of God; the throne in Scripture indicates kingship (cf. 1 Chr 29:23, "and Solomon sat on the throne of the Lord"). The corporealists have agreed with us that God has never been in a place; they hold that God created the place and did not change — and just as before creation He was not in a place, so after creation He is not in a place.

Ps 91:4: "He shall cover thee with His pinions, and under His wings shalt thou take refuge" — does anyone permit himself to predicate feathers or wings of God? Isa 59:17: "He put on righteousness as a breastplate, and a helmet of salvation upon His head" — these are acts, and acts are not worn; the language of "wearing" is figurative, since what is worn is garments. Similarly "helmet of salvation upon His head" — not a literal head in the bodily-organic sense; just as helmet is not a literal physical item, but a figure for the act of help and rescue.

There remain two questions: Gen 1:26 ("let us make man in our image, after our likeness") and Num 12:8 ("mouth to mouth I speak with him"). We have responded in our commentary on Gen 1:1. Our preferred answers are two: Answer 1: Gen 1:26–27 (and other "image" passages) is to be read honorific-elevatively: God created all things, and singled out one part of His creation — namely humanity — and named it specially, calling it His [image] of [Himself]. As He calls one piece of land My land (Jer 2:7, Hos 9:3); one of His mountains My mountain (Ps 68:16, Isa 49:11); one of His houses My house (Isa 56:7, "for My house shall be called a house of prayer for all peoples") — so He created the various forms and selected one — the human form — and named it His form.

The second answer: that Adam is in God's image and likeness with respect to sovereignty and dominion, not with respect to image and likeness of body. Just as one says, "so-and-so is in the image of a learned man" or "so-and-so is in the image of a sufi" — without meaning that he is physically like them, but rather that he has the rank and station of one. God made Adam, of all things, the sovereign over all, owning over the rest — just as God Himself is the absolute Sovereign owner of all. Confirmed by what immediately follows "in our image" (Gen 1:26): "and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea and the birds of the air … etc." So He informed that the resemblance is in dominion, not anywhere else. So David said (Ps 8:7): "and thou hast given him dominion over the works of Thy hands"; preceded by (Ps 8:6): "and Thou hast made him a little lower than the angels" — i.e., He lacks the acquisition and creative-discovery and similar things [that the angels possess in higher degree].

As to Num 12:8 ("mouth to mouth I speak with him") — God (mighty and exalted) addresses prophets in two modes: through an angel (the standard mode), and in a dream (as He addressed Jacob and others). Some have held that there is a third mode — inspiration (ilhām) and occurrence-to-the-heart; we have no need to settle that here. God (mighty and exalted) honored Moses in particular and singled him out from the rest of the prophets in this mode: namely, He created a spoken utterance and placed it in some material — air, or fire, or whatever — making Himself by that the speaker-with-Moses, just as one human being addresses another from his mouth — until the speech enters the other's mouth — that is, face-to-face speaking without intermediary. As Jacob testifies (Gen 32:31), "I have seen God face to face." Confirming our reading: Scripture immediately before (Num 12:6) says: "if there be a prophet of you, I the Lord shall make Myself known to him in a vision" — meaning, for other prophets I make Myself known in vision; in dreams I speak with him. They see angels; not so My servant Moses; he is the exception, distinguished — I speak with him face to face, by the creating of speech without intermediary.

Some who hold that speech is eternal might press: if you say God creates speech in something other than Himself, by which He becomes a speaker — why not say He creates motion, color, and death in something other than Himself, by which He becomes moved, colored, dead? This is not the place to settle this. We will treat it in the bab on the Christians (who hold that the word is eternal — i.e., the Word of God, "Christ"). For the present: a thing is not dead because it created death in another; not moved or colored because it created motion or color in another. Were that so, an inanimate thing — which is what creates motion in its own parts — would itself be motioned. But many things are moved and colored and deceased without themselves having caused these states. So the inherence of the state (motion, color, death) is what produces the predication; not the causing of the state. Speech, by contrast: the speaker is precisely the one who performs the act of speaking; every one who performs the act is a speaker, commanding, prohibiting. This argument also returns against those who hold that speech is eternal alongside God; we will pursue this in its place.[{3}]

If someone further asks about what follows Num 12:8 — "and the likeness of the Lord he beholds": this also suggests visibility. Reply: this parallels Gen 9:6, "for in the image of God He made man" — where "image of God" does not mean God's image in His essence, but the image He owns, by way of ownership. So here "the likeness of God he beholds" refers to the forms God owns — that is, the angels. If they say: but angels are seen by many prophets — what then is the special distinction of Moses? Reply: two answers. First: Moses' distinction is not this seeing-of-the-angels, but rather "mouth to mouth I speak with him"; the phrase "the likeness of the Lord he beholds" is adjoined to indicate, additionally, that he saw the angels as other prophets saw them, and also received the special mode of speech-without-intermediary. Second: Moses may have seen and beheld some of the angels closer and more proximate to God (higher-ranking angels) than the angels that ordinary prophets see — for those higher angels do not come down to earth. Of the two answers, the first is, in my view, the stronger. --- The Second Maqāla is completed; with its completion ends the first part of the book. The Third Maqāla — on the refutation of the [Christian] sects and their statements — will follow in the second part. With God is power, and He is sufficient for me; how excellent the Disposer.[{4}] ---
